activities.anchor: Behind every manipulation, exercise programme and
activities.caption: file each observation under its science
activities.name: physLangSort

config.prompt: Three languages for one case — the patient who cannot rise from a low chair. File each observation:

items.label: rising needs large hip and knee torques from a deep-flexion position, where leverage is poor
the armrests are simply adding force at a long moment arm
can the quadriceps generate the needed force at all?
eight weeks of progressive sit-to-stand training can add the missing torque
many patients shift their weight too far back, loading the weakest position
a cue — 'nose over toes' — changes the task more cheaply than any strength gain could

config.why: Weak, unfit or unskilled? Usually a little of each, in different proportions per patient — which is why the three sciences are taught together.

activities.caption: true or false — the lactic acid story
activities.name: physDomsJudge

statements.s: Next-day muscle soreness is caused by a buildup of lactic acid.
statements.why: The lactate produced in hard exercise is cleared within the hour — and it is a fuel and signalling molecule.

statements.s: DOMS is micro-damage and inflammation from unaccustomed eccentric loading.
statements.why: The mistake matters clinically: patients who believe in 'acid buildup' stretch, rest excessively or avoid the very progressive loading that would adapt their muscles.

statements.s: Lactate is cleared within the hour after hard exercise.
statements.why: It never lingers to poison muscles the next morning.

statements.s: Soreness is a warning to stop training altogether.
statements.why: DOMS accompanies adaptation — avoided progressive loading is the real clinical cost of the myth.

activities.anchor: Prescription turns this physiology into a dose
activities.caption: place the marker at the patient's training heart rate
activities.name: physKarvonenPlace

config.prompt: A 50-year-old, resting heart rate 70 (Tanaka HRmax = 208 − 0.7 × 50 = 173), training at 60 per cent of heart-rate reserve (Karvonen). Place the target heart rate:
config.why: 70 + 0.6 × (173 − 70) ≈ 132 beats per minute — a number the patient can watch on any pulse monitor, which is what makes physiology clinical rather than academic.

activities.caption: walk the bed-rest finding into a prescription
activities.name: physBedrestBranch

config.root: The Dallas bed-rest studies: young subjects lost roughly a quarter to a third of their aerobic capacity in three weeks of strict bed rest. Walk the prescription logic.

start.text: Which principle does the finding instantiate?

choices.label: Specificity — adaptations are specific to what is trained
Reversibility — adaptation is rented, not owned

spec.text: True — cycling fitness transfers imperfectly to running — but the bed-rest loss is the other principle: deconditioning obeys the dose–response law in reverse.

rev.text: Reversibility. So what follows for post-surgical and post-stroke care?

choices.label: Rest until the patient feels ready
Early mobilisation as a prescription with doses and targets

rest.text: That is the pre-evidence habit — and three weeks of strict rest is precisely what cost the Dallas subjects a quarter to a third of their capacity.

early.text: Early mobilisation with doses and targets — 'just keep moving' is the most evidence-based sentence in the profession.

config.why: Specificity shapes what to train; reversibility is why waiting is itself a dose — the wrong one.

activities.caption: find the faulty line in this student's deconditioning note
activities.name: physFatSpot

config.prompt: One line of this student's deconditioning note is wrong — click it:
lines: Muscle and fat are different tissues — fibres cannot transmute into adipocytes.
On deconditioning, muscle fibre atrophy runs alongside fat gain from an energy balance without training.
The two processes run in parallel and are separately reversible.
Stopped training, muscle converts to fat — which is why ex-athletes get heavy.
Renewed progressive loading rebuilds muscle rather than 'converting' anything.
config.correction: Nothing converts: fibre atrophy and energy-balance fat gain are separate processes — each one reversible on its own.
config.why: Reversibility in the language of physiology — not transmutation of tissue.

activities.anchor: if the nervous system cannot deploy them
activities.caption: sequence Fitts and Posner's stages of motor learning
activities.name: physStagesOrder

items: Cognitive — performing by thinking: effortful, error-ridden
Autonomous — performed while attention is elsewhere: standing up while holding a conversation
config.why: Each stage wants a different clinic: instructions and demonstration early, variable challenge in the middle, real-world dual-task practice at the end.

activities.anchor: where the science earns its keep
activities.caption: pair each practice-design finding with its consequence
activities.name: physPracticeMatch

config.prompt: Counter-intuitive but confirmed — pair each finding with its consequence:

pairs.right: feels worse and retains better — the contextual-interference effect
forces the patient to develop their own intrinsic error detection — the capacity they need at home

config.why: Schema theory: the motor program is tuned by comparing predicted with actual sensory consequences, so the system learns most from variability and error.

activities.caption: bet before you read on — ten thousand flawless reps
activities.name: physPerfectPredict

config.q: A patient rehearses a compensatory pattern — the hitched shoulder, the locked knee — ten thousand times, flawlessly. What has practice made?
choices: Perfect — flawless repetition fixes the pattern
Permanent — a compensation harder to unlearn than the original skill would have been to acquire
Nothing — flawless repetitions do not change the motor program
Whatever the therapist's feedback schedule decides
config.why: Practice makes permanent — of whatever was practised. Quality and variability of practice outrank quantity, the quiet revolution of motor-learning research.
